source: Mehmet can (2026) Falsification, Not Exposure: placebo-controlled decomposition of self-repair feedback in frozen small code models
finding: Matched-budget test of what in a repair prompt actually helps. On tasks where no sample in a best-of-8 pool passed, blind resampling beat re-showing the bare failing code. Failing code plus real execution facts only tied blind resampling. Own near-miss code and runtime traces tied a content-free placebo in follow-ups.
numbers: 290 dead task-model units, 6 benchmark-model cells (HumanEval+, MBPP+), 3 models of 0.5B-1.5B, 7,000 fresh generations plus 1,400 follow-up. Blind resampling beat bare-code retry by +18 net unlocks (discordant 25/7, Holm p=0.0021). Code+facts beat bare code by +18 (21/3, p=0.00042) and beat a same-code generic-bullet placebo by +15 (p=0.0041). Code+facts and blind resampling both unlocked 26 pooled. Instruction-only effect +3, p=0.36 (not distinguishable).
quote: valuable not as Popperian vocabulary, verbal self-critique, or re-exposure to failing code
limits: Tiny frozen models only. Internally preregistered by one author, single preprint, not peer reviewed. Authors say the tie is not evidence of equivalence. The content-vs-form contrast flipped direction in a small disjoint sample. Output-budget matched, not wall-clock.
agent_relevance: Directly answers part of gap 1 for weak models: repair is not better than fresh samples. Re-showing a failed draft without new facts is the worst arm. If our agent repairs, it should feed in new execution facts, or resample.

source: Li et al. (2025) S*: Test Time Scaling for Code Generation (Tables 1 and 2)
finding: On LiveCodeBench v2 the gain from two rounds of self-debugging on public tests shrinks and can turn negative for reasoning models, while 16-sample majority vote and the full S* hybrid gain far more. Not equal compute: S* and majority vote use many samples, self-debug uses one.
limits: Self-debug is a single sample with 2 rounds, so it is far cheaper than the other columns; this is a coverage-and-cost mix, not a matched-token test. Table printed with merged cells; column mapping checked against the deltas in the abstract (+24.7, +19.6, +14.3, +8.6). Small non-frontier reasoning models. Competition programming, not repo debugging.
agent_relevance: Partial answer to gap 6: for reasoning models, self-debug on public tests adds +1.0 (R1-32B), +3.4 (o1-mini), -2.8 (QwQ). Gap 1 stays open for a matched-token test, but sampling plus selection wins at the cost S* pays.

source: Li et al. (2025) S*: ablations on debugging variants and selection policy (Sections 5.3 and 5.4)
finding: Reasoning models still gain a little from explicit execution-feedback debugging. Adding model-written tests to the public tests during debugging did not help. Model-written tests as a selector did not beat public tests alone. A selector that asks the model to invent distinguishing INPUTS and then reads real execution OUTPUTS did best.
numbers: QwQ-32B-Preview Pass@N 72.6 to 74.2 with 2 debug rounds (N=8, up to 5 rounds plotted). Selection Pass@1 on LiveCodeBench v4, averages: public tests only 53.8, generated tests 53.1, LLM judge 55.6. The adaptive-input-synthesis cells in the same table are misaligned in the PDF text, so its figure is not used here. Last-round-only context helped Qwen-7B and hurt the other two.
limits: Gains of 1-2 points on one benchmark, no variance reported. The authors chose 2 rounds for simplicity after seeing returns flatten. Table 3 text is scrambled.
agent_relevance: Gap 4: model-written tests are a weak filter when real public tests exist, and the better design avoids predicting outputs at all. Our agent should compare candidates by running them on invented inputs and reading real outputs, not by asserting expected values.

source: Song, Raiman, Catanzaro (2024) Effective Large Language Model Debugging with Best-first Tree Search (BESTER)
finding: A matched-inference-call comparison (21 calls each) of plain sampling, execution-feedback repair, Reflexion and best-first search. Simple repair loops often fall below plain sampling at equal calls. Search that follows the branch passing the most tests is best in 8 of 9 cells.
numbers: Pass@Infer at 21 calls, sampling / ex-feedback / Reflexion / BESTER. GPT-4 HumanEval 82.67 / 88.41 / 89.02 / 90.24; MBPP 78.30 / 80.69 / 78.04 / 81.48; APPS 67.85 / 69.33 / 69.33 / 72.33. DeepSeek HumanEval 74.46 / 73.78 / 73.17 / 81.71; APPS 57.54 / 53.67 / 50.67 / 54.67 (all three feedback methods below sampling). Llama3 MBPP 73.14 / 71.96 / 72.49 / 74.07. Selection rule on DeepSeek HumanEval: random repair 75.61, most-passing-tests 81.71. Best tree shape N=2 rounds with k=5 reflections.
limits: The text does not say how the sampling baseline is scored at 21 calls (pass@21 against hidden tests or selected); read the sampling column with care. 2024 models, one group, no variance. The search needs visible tests to rank branches.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 3. At equal calls, plain repair is not reliably better than sampling, and picking the next branch by test pass count is what matters. Middle depth beats very deep or very shallow.

source: Ehrlich, Brown, Juravsky, Clark, Re, Mirhoseini (2025) CodeMonkeys: Scaling Test-Time Compute for Software Engineering (serial vs parallel)
finding: On SWE-bench Verified the authors swept iterations per trajectory (serial) against trajectories per issue (parallel). After the first few iterations and samples, configurations of equal cost had similar coverage. Serial depth cannot rescue a run whose model already approved its own wrong work; a new parallel sample gives a fresh start.
numbers: 10 testing+editing state machines x up to 8 iterations gave coverage 69.8% (any candidate correct), Claude Sonnet 3.5. Final selected score 57.4% at about 2,300 USD. Context step (LLM reads every file) under 15% of cost. DeepSeek-V3 repeat in the appendix: coverage still rising with samples.
quote: Increasing the iteration limit further does not help "stuck" state machines where models have already incorrectly approved of their work.
limits: Coverage uses SWE-bench tests as oracle. Serial scaling is only indirect (a cap on iterations; models may stop early). One system, 2024 model, Verified set (leakage risk). Two configurations with equal coverage can differ after selection.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 3: closest thing to an equal-cost serial-vs-parallel curve on a real debugging task. Supports a stop rule of a few rounds, then restart with a fresh sample rather than a deeper loop on the same draft.

source: Ehrlich et al. (2025) CodeMonkeys: selection among candidate edits (Section 2.3)
finding: Selection, not generation, was the bottleneck. Majority voting with model-written tests beat random choice; asking a model to pick without that filter was worse than the vote; filtering to the top 3 by test votes and then running a selection loop that writes new distinguishing tests worked best.
numbers: Random selection expected 45.8%; oracle (coverage) 69.8%; final 57.4%, closing about half the random-to-oracle gap. Selection state machine under 10% of total cost. Ensemble of existing top Verified submissions: coverage 80.8%, selected 66.2%, above the best member.
limits: Model-written tests here reproduce the issue (no public test exists), which differs from S* where public tests exist. Single system. Verified has leakage and weak tests (see d20).
agent_relevance: Gap 4, in part: agent-written tests are a good FILTER over many candidates when no real test exists, and the selection step must use execution, not model opinion. They are a poor lone stop signal for one draft (Reflexion MBPP, evidence a11).

source: Brown, Juravsky, Ehrlich, Clark, Le, Re, Mirhoseini (2024) Large Language Monkeys: Scaling Inference Compute with Repeated Sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) rises steadily with sample count, and it converts to real accuracy only when a verifier can pick the right sample. Unit tests can; majority vote and reward models cannot keep up and plateau.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples (single-sample state of the art then 43%). On GSM8K and MATH with Llama-3-8B and 70B, majority vote and reward-model best-of-N plateau near 100 samples while coverage passes 95% at 10,000 samples.
limits: Coverage is scored by the benchmark's own tests, so 56% is an upper bound for a deployable system. The verifier plateau was measured on math, not code. The paper itself notes false positives from weak tests.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 background. The value of sampling depends on the quality of the independent check. If our agent's check is weak, extra samples give no real gain, and repair on one draft is just as weak.

source: Li (2026) Decomposing LLM Self-Correction: the Accuracy-Correction Paradox and Error Depth Hypothesis
finding: Splitting self-correction into detect, localise, correct: detection does not predict correction, and the model's own localisation hints lowered correction for two of three models. Iterative reflection (up to 3 rounds) fixed far more, which the author reads as repeated re-solving. Weaker models corrected more of their errors than the strongest model.
numbers: GSM8K-Complex, n=500 per model, 346 errors. Intrinsic correction / with own location hint / iterative(3). DeepSeek (94% accuracy, 30 errors) 16.7 / 26.7 / 20.0. GPT-3.5 (66.4%, 168 errors) 26.8 / 15.5 / 67.9; detection 81.5%. Claude (70.4%, 148 errors) 29.1 / 12.8 / 60.8; detection 10.1%.
quote: Surprisingly, providing error location hints hurts all models.
limits: The abstract says hints hurt all models, but the paper's own table shows DeepSeek improving 16.7 to 26.7 (n=30, wide interval), so the claim is overstated. Hints are model-generated, not ground truth. Math, not code. Single-author preprint. Iterative gain may be plain resampling.
agent_relevance: Gap 2, negative side: a naive 'name the faulty step, then fix it' operator that trusts the model's own localisation can lower repair. Measure localisation accuracy first; do not feed an unverified location into the rewrite.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) Structure Enables Effective Self-Localization of Errors in LLMs (Thought-ICS)
finding: If reasoning is written as discrete, complete thoughts, models localise their own first wrong step more accurately than in free-form chain of thought, and backtracking to the last good thought then resampling works. Given an oracle that says the answer is wrong, this gives 20-40% lift. Localisation in unstructured traces drifts to later segments than the reference.
numbers: Models 3B-120B, math, science and commonsense benchmarks. Oracle-verified lift 20-40%. The localisation reference is a consensus of three frontier models (agreement with token-level spans only 58% at a 10% length tolerance), not human labels.
quote: It remains unclear whether such methods constitute genuine self-correction or succeed through structured resampling.
limits: Not code. The oracle tells the loop the answer is wrong, so detection is free. The authors say it is unclear whether the gain is genuine self-correction or structured resampling. Models up to 120B only.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: first measured support for a 'first wrong step' operator, with a condition: the trace must be written in separable steps. Our agent should write its debug reasoning as numbered steps if it is to localise errors in them.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) Thought-ICS: self-verification as the bottleneck (Section 6.1, Table 1)
finding: When the model itself decides whether to keep correcting, the loop breaks more correct answers than it fixes, under every gating rule tried. Specificity (leaving correct answers alone) collapses with each extra iteration.
numbers: 9 samples per iteration. Recall / specificity / broke / fixed (percent of initially correct answers broken, of initially incorrect answers fixed): Single 68.3 / 66.9 / 10.9 / 6.2; Any 94.6 / 30.9 / 21.4 / 8.1; Majority 70.2 / 69.9 / 12.7 / 6.3; Unanimous 34.7 / 94.6 / 6.0 / 3.5.
limits: Averages across models and datasets, math and reasoning tasks, not code. A confidence-safeguard variant gave positive net lift in the paper (figure only, not read in detail).
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 4: continuing after a self-judged failure is dangerous. A stop rule needs an outside signal, or a rule that keeps the first draft unless the second beats it on an independent check.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: First-error localisation improved sharply with reasoning-trained models. Prompted critics find the earliest wrong step, and the best reasoning model is far ahead of a strong non-reasoning model.
numbers: 3,400 test cases with human-annotated earliest-error step; F1 of error-case and correct-case accuracy. Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o-0806 61.9. QwQ-32B-Preview is the best open model, competitive with GPT-4o but behind o1-mini.
limits: Math (GSM8K to Olympiad), not code. A different task from BIG-Bench Mistake (Tyen, 52.87 for GPT-4), so the numbers cannot be compared directly. Per-subset table cells are scrambled in the PDF text; only the figure averages are used.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: the 52.87 figure for GPT-4 is probably stale for modern reasoning models. First-step localisation is much better in reasoning models, so the operator is more plausible now. No code-specific equivalent measured.

source: Tsui (2026) Self-Correction Bench, COLM 2026 version (re-opened)
finding: The blind spot is a property of non-reasoning models. Reasoning models show a small or even negative blind spot: they fix their own injected errors as well as errors in the user turn. Appending 'Wait' to a non-reasoning model lifts it to near its reasoning twin.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: 64.5% average blind spot; 'Wait' cuts it 89.3% and raises mean accuracy 156%. DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-70B blind spot 0.113 (SCLI5), -0.031 (GSM8K-SC), -0.05 (PRM800K-SC). Accuracy base / +Wait / reasoning twin: DeepSeek-V3 0.567 / 0.902 / 0.908; Qwen3-14B 0.117 / 0.868 / 0.843; Qwen3-32B 0.045 / 0.793 / 0.894. On models' own natural errors, at least 4.3-10.8% were errors the model could have caught.
quote: Reasoning models exhibit a small, even negative, Self-Correction Blind Spot
limits: Injected errors in short math and logic tasks; the magnitude is a property of the design, not a deployment rate. Single author, 1,024-token cap, no code tasks. No equal-token control for 'Wait' (it adds tokens).
agent_relevance: Gap 5: for a modern reasoning model, a colleague-framing trick is probably unnecessary because post-training already covers it. Keep it as a cheap option only for non-reasoning or short-output modes. Test on code before assuming.

source: Gandhi, Tsay, Ganhotra, Kate, Rizk (2025) When Agents go Astray: Course-Correcting SWE Agents with PRMs (SWE-PRM)
finding: A separate model watches the agent's last steps for looping, redundant search and subgoal drift, and injects feedback. A strong outside monitor raised resolution on SWE-bench Verified. Open-weight monitors, including a same-size model, did not. Feedback grounded in a failure taxonomy beat free critique and beat explicit action orders.
numbers: Base SWE-agent-LM-32B 40.0% resolved at 2.77 USD per 100 instances, 38.64 steps. With a Claude Sonnet 4 monitor: unguided 45.8% (51.54 steps, 28.42 USD), taxonomy-guided 50.6% (37.99 steps, 25.98 USD), taxonomy plus action recommendation 44.8% (34.38 steps). Open-source monitors 30.0-38.8%. Sonnet 4 as the policy alone: 66.6% at 121.66 USD per 100.
limits: Not equal compute: cost rose about 9x. A stronger policy alone beat every monitor setup in accuracy. Workshop paper, Verified set (leakage risk), no repeated runs stated. The monitor is a stronger model than the policy, so it is not a self-monitor.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: supports an external stop-and-redirect check, but only from a model stronger than the actor. Same-strength monitoring did not help. Telling the agent exactly what to do made it worse than naming the problem.

source: Liu, Chen, Krishna, Sinha, Ganhotra, Jabbarvand (2026) Process-Centric Analysis of Agentic Software Systems (Graphectory and online monitor)
finding: A rule-based monitor on SWE-agent detects loops, plan violations and long stagnation, drops the offending step, and sends a short diagnostic. On trajectories that had shown problems twice, it cut loops by over 90% and raised resolution. Plan violations were much harder to change than loops.
numbers: 4,000 trajectories analysed (SWE-agent and OpenHands, 4 models, SWE-bench Verified). Monitor test on 86 reproducible problematic cases out of 153. Resolution vanilla to monitored: DeepSeek-R1 11.8 to 35.3 (+23.5, n=17); DeepSeek-V3 8.7 to 21.7 (+13.0, n=23); Devstral 10.9 to 17.8 (+6.9, n=46). Steps fell by 11.5 to 59.9 (percent). Stagnation rule: at least 5 navigation steps with no edit.
quote: A repeating cycle of actions is detected. Summarize the failing behavior and choose one decisive next step.
limits: Selection effect: instances were chosen because vanilla runs showed problems in at least two of three repeats, and vanilla counts as resolved only if ALL repeats resolve, while the monitored arm is a fresh run. This inflates the gain through regression to the mean. Small n. No equal-token control.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: gives concrete cheap triggers (a cycle of repeated actions; 5 steps without an edit) and message wording that agents follow. Treat +7 to +23 as an upper bound until replicated on unselected tasks.

source: Yuan et al. (2025) debug-gym: A Text-Based Environment for Interactive Debugging
finding: Giving an agent a real debugger (pdb) helps strong models on repo-level bugs and can hurt weaker ones. Giving pdb only after 5 failed rewrites worked better than from step one, for the models tested. On simple tasks (Aider) pdb added nothing.
numbers: 3 runs each, SWE-bench Lite. Claude 3.7 Sonnet success: rewrite-only 37.2, debug 48.4, debug(5) 52.1. Text: for weaker models (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B) early pdb 'could to some extent harm'; debug(5) beat rewrite in all cases. Aider (133 tasks): o3-mini 95.2 rewrite vs 94.2 debug. Mini-nightmare (10 tasks): strong models at 90-100 for all arms.
quote: returns gradually diminish, and the final few rewrites bring virtually no value
limits: Table 3 cells in the PDF text are misaligned, so only the Claude row is quoted; other cell values are not used. Prompt-only agents with minimal tool instructions; the authors say models lack debugging-trace training. No token-matched control, though response tokens rose little. Small benchmarks.
agent_relevance: Gaps 7 and 3: best evidence that runtime probes beat read-and-rerun for strong models on hard repo bugs, and that 'after 5 failed rewrites, switch tool' beats always-on. Weak models should not get the probe tool.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Coherence Collapse: Diagnosing Why Code Agents Fail After Reaching the Right Code (TRAJEVAL)
finding: Most failures of strong models are not about finding the code. They reach and edit the right function and still end with a wrong patch. The biggest single sub-type is overwriting or thrashing a correct edit. In 5 cases the agent had written a patch identical to the gold patch and later destroyed it.
numbers: 16,758 trajectories, 3 scaffolds, 7 models. SWE-agent on Verified, 1,607 failures: Search 19.3%, Read 9.0%, Edit-target 14.8%, Edit-quality 56.9% (GPT-5 68.1%). Of 914 edit-quality failures: coherence collapse 39.7% (22.6% of all failures; confused thrashing 29.1%, near-correct corrupted 10.6%), wrong branch point 18.6%, wrong function in file 17.6%, partial understanding 7.3%, incomplete fix 7.0%. Edit-commit checkpoint recovered 5 of 5 exact cases. Consensus feedback from 3-of-6 other models on viewed files: GPT-5 66.0% to 69.0% (+3.0, McNemar p=0.08, n=500; 39 gained, 24 lost; precision 52.4%); gold-patch oracle +4.6 (p<.001).
quote: the agent reaches correct code and then overwrites or thrashes it
limits: Labels partly automated; second-author agreement kappa 0.80 on 3 classes and 0.71 on 5. Reference-patch alignment assumes one right location. Consensus gain not significant. Verified set, leakage risk.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: separates 'slip' (overwritten correct edit, 22.6% of failures) from 'wrong design' (wrong branch point about 10% of all failures, plus partial understanding). Suggests a keep-best-so-far guard (checkpoint passing edits) is worth more than an abandon-approach operator.

source: Majgaonkar, Fei, Li, Sarro, Ye (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: Success and Failure Trajectories (re-opened)
finding: Failed trajectories are longer and have much wider spread than successful ones. Most failed runs still touch the right file, so success hinges on exact versus approximate edits.
numbers: OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus on SWE-bench Lite and Verified. SWE-agent failures 12.6% longer (Lite) and 18.5% longer (Verified); OpenHands 31.0% and 82.5% longer; Prometheus 56.6% and 50.7% longer. Correct-file rate 72-81% even in failures. Step-count standard deviation in Lite 100.79 vs 34.62 for one agent.
limits: Observational: a long run is a symptom of a hard task as well as a cause of failure. This re-open confirms c23; it is the same paper, not independent of it.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: length alone is not a usable stop rule because it confuses hard tasks with stuck ones. Use content triggers (repeats, no edits) as in d14.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) SWE-bench Goes Live!
finding: A fresh benchmark of issues created since 2024 gives resolve rates less than half those on SWE-bench Verified for the same agent and model under the same protocol. Agents did better on repos already in SWE-bench, and issue recency showed no clear effect.
numbers: 1,319 tasks, 93 repositories. Best: OpenHands with Claude 3.7 Sonnet, 19.25% on the full set (17.67% Lite); the same pair re-run on Verified with identical setup: 43.20%. Repos from SWE-bench 22.96% vs new repos 18.89% (instance counts in Table 5 are garbled in the PDF text). No clear trend across quarters 2024Q1 to 2025Q1.
quote: the highest resolved rate on SWE-bench-Live is only 19.25%
limits: The gap is partly different task difficulty, not a clean contamination estimate. Model training cutoffs were not matched to issue dates.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: expect about half the headline score on unseen repos. Report our agent on a rolling post-cutoff set alongside any public benchmark and compare the ratio.

source: Deng, Da et al. (2025) SWE-Bench Pro: Can AI Agents Solve Long-Horizon Software Engineering Tasks?
finding: A benchmark built from copyleft-licensed repos (public and held-out sets) and private startup repos (commercial set). Scores are far lower on the private commercial set. Failure-mode shares differ by model, so one agent loop cannot be tuned for all.
numbers: 1,865 problems, 41 repos; public set 731, commercial set 276. Public Pass@1 with SWE-agent: Claude Sonnet 4.5 43.6, Sonnet 4 42.7, GPT-5 (high) 41.8. Commercial: Opus 4.1 17.8, GPT-5 (high) 15.7, GPT-5 (medium) 14.9, Sonnet 4 9.1. Failures (LLM judge on last 20 turns): Opus 4.1 wrong solution 35.9% and syntax error 24.2%; Sonnet 4 context overflow 35.6%.
limits: Another table in the same PDF (50 turns, 2 USD cap) shows GPT-5 high at 25.9, so scores depend on limits; numbers here are Tables 1 and 2 of the v2 copy opened. The judge is an LLM (GPT-5). Prompts are augmented with requirements.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the private commercial split is the closest public example of a hidden-test, unseen-code design. The public-to-private drop is about 2x to 4x depending on model.

source: Aleithan et al. (2024) SWE-Bench+: Enhanced Coding Benchmark for LLMs (re-opened)
finding: On re-opening: leaked solutions and weak tests inflate SWE-bench. Of resolved patches, a third copied the answer from the issue text or comments, and about another third were suspicious because tests were weak. Filtering cut the resolve rate for SWE-agent with GPT-4 from 12.47% to 3.97%.
numbers: 32.67% of passed patches involved solution leakage (82 patches). 31.08% suspicious due to weak tests. Resolve rate 12.47% to 3.97% after refinement. Incorrect fixes 12.75% and incomplete fixes 3.59% listed in the same table.
limits: The 31.08% weak-test figure differs from the PatchDiff 29.6%; they measure different things (suspicious patches vs behaviour differences among resolved) with different agents. One agent, GPT-4 era.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: any internal evaluation should check that the answer is not in the issue text and that hidden tests are stronger than the agent's own.

source: Kang, An, Yoo (2024) AutoFL: explanation quality and confidence (re-opened)
finding: On re-opening, the explanation-quality figures hold, and there is no ablation that removes the explanation or compares it to re-reading. Confidence from repeated runs correlates with localisation quality.
numbers: Manual review of 300 explanations from 60 bugs: about 20% accurately describe how the bug happened; 56.7% of bugs had at least one accurate explanation. Method-level acc@1 up to 233.3% over Ochiai with GPT-4 on BugsInPy. Spearman between confidence and performance up to 0.57 (Defects4J) and 0.52 (BugsInPy). Developers liked few, high-quality explanations; redundant content and wrong fix suggestions misled them.
limits: No arm without explanation, so explain-first versus locate-first is not isolated. Fault localisation, not repair. Defects4J and BugsInPy are public and likely seen in training.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open: no study I could open isolates rubber-duck explanation from re-reading when a test is present. A wrong explanation can mislead a human; for an agent, require the explanation to name a check that could refute it.
